newsitem.title: USA: Merck drug seen as future migraine leader.
newsitem.headline: Merck drug seen as future migraine leader.

text.p: Analysts predicted Wednesday a new migraine drug being developed by Merck and Co could eventually displace Glaxo Wellcome Plc's sumatriptan as the drug of choice, but said the new drug is likely to expand the market rather than threaten Glaxo's market share.

Merck, in a statement earlier Wednesday from Amsterdam, said a study had shown that its new oral migraine drug Maxalt (rizatriptan benzoate) provided significantly faster and more complete pain relief than Glaxo's drug, which had worldwide sales of $840 million in 1996.
The news helped lift Merck's shares 1-1/2 to 95-5/8 in afternoon trading. Glaxo's shares closed at 1277 p, up 5 p.

Merck said an international study of 1,099 patients showed that 10 mg tablets of Maxalt, now under development, helped more patients become pain-free within two hours than 100 mg of sumatriptan, which Glaxo markets as Imitrex in the U.S. and Imigran in Europe.

HKS & Co analyst Hemant Shah said Merck's drug, expected to be submitted for U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval within the next few months, will have the advantage of fewer cardiovascular side effects than Glaxo's drug.

"The Merck drug will expand the market because a lot of people can't use the Glaxo drug due to side effects," Shah said, with the potential of at least $200 million in annual sales if approved by the FDA.
"But Glaxo won't lose its migraine market share because the market is so untapped. Imitrex will continue to grow," he said.
Shah added that a handful of other migraine drugs are expected to also hit the market in the next two years, including products from Pfizer Inc and SmithKline Beecham Plc.
Smith Barney analyst Joshua Alpert said Maxalt was one of the "hot drugs" in Merck's pipeline, which he projected could have worldwide sales of $700 million by 2001.
"Maxalt has a little better efficacy than Glaxo, so it will become the drug of choice," Alpert said.

Ramona Jones, a Glaxo spokeswoman, said she had not yet seen results of the comparative study. But she said her company's drug had a clear advantage of being available in injection form, with pain relief beginning to take effect within 10 minutes.
She said about 26 million Americans are believed to suffer from migraines, with only 10 million now under physician's care.
About 2.5 million people in the United States take the Glaxo drug, she added.

Jones said Imitrex was Glaxo's second-best-selling drug in the United States, behind the blockbuster Zantac ulcer medication which had sales of $1.6 billion in the United States and $3 billion worldwide.
But the key U.S. patent for Zantac expires in July, just three months after the patent expiration on another Glaxo blockbuster, the anti-viral Zovirax.
